## What this is

Each notebook here answers one question of the form *"how does SIFT compare
against X?"*, where X is a specific piece of existing work. They exist so that
what we try, and what we learn, is written down and reproducible — including the
things that turned out to be wrong.

They are **not part of the manuscript**. The paper stays focused on making a
baby out of conjoint and search; these are the working notes behind it. The one
notebook that *is* part of the manuscript,
[`notebooks/sift_likelihood.qmd`](../notebooks/sift_likelihood.qmd), is there
because it documents the paper's own estimator rather than a comparison.

## How they work

Each comparison is a pair:

- `exp_<name>.R` — the experiment. Run **from the repo root**
  (`Rscript comparisons/exp_<name>.R`); writes its result to
  `comparisons/out/<name>.rds`.
- `compare-<name>.qmd` — the write-up. Loads the saved result and displays it.

Splitting them this way means the notebooks render in seconds and always show
numbers that were actually produced, never numbers that were typed in.

Shared setup lives in [`_common.R`](_common.R).

## What these have already changed

Two claims in the paper were corrected because of work done here, which is the
point of keeping the record.

The **simulator comparison** retired a headline of "399× lower simulation
variance". It was measured before a fix to the likelihood and on six
replications; re-measured properly it is 21–100×, design-dependent, and the
defensible claim is precision-per-second of 3–21×.

The **position comparison** reversed a sign. The draft asserted that a flat
relationship between position and purchase-conditional-on-click rules out
position entering pre-search utility. Simulation shows the opposite: selection
makes that relationship strongly *positive* when position acts on costs, and
flat when it acts on utility. Reading it the intuitive way inverts the
conclusion.
